title: Diversity hawks defeated to halt private markets rush
full_text:
The ASX has gone back to basics on its corporate governance principles, burying an ambitious diversity agenda that called for company directors to make public their sexuality and religion.
The market operator on Tuesday opened consultation on its fifth edition of Australia’s corporate governance principles, which retain the 30 per cent female target for ASX boards. A new advisory group was brought in following the disbanding of the more than two-decade-old Corporate Governance Council that became the target of a corporate outcry.
The 19-member council got into strife last year when it proposed an extension of diversity characteristics to include race, sexual orientation, religious beliefs and socio-economic background. Supportive members included the Association of Superannuation Funds of Australia.
A new eight-member committee, led by former Reserve Bank governor Philip Lowe, is proposing to de-emphasise the diversity aspect of the guidelines.
Board diversity targets for ASX 300 companies will remain unchanged, with the aim for women to make up 30 per cent of board seats, but additional targets for other diversity characteristics, or disclosure of these, have been abandoned.
Dr Lowe said the advisory group took a commonsense perspective on gender targets but also wanted to broaden out the discussion of diversity.
“We want to talk about diversity of education, people’s backgrounds, skills, and perspectives, to move the diversity discussion beyond just gender,” he told The Australian.
“That’s what’s going to bring a good board … from a very common sense-based perspective, that’s what’s going to give the best long-term value creation for companies.
“Setting targets or objectives for sexual orientation, I don’t think is going to do that.” Critics of the old governance council, including investor John Wylie, memorably blasted the prescriptive aspect of the mooted governance principles. Dr Lowe said he did not want to discourage private companies from listing on the public market by going too far. “If you make these principles too prescriptive and not fit the purpose for the 1900 companies that are on the stock exchange, it becomes a disincentive to list on the stock exchange,” he said.
“If you push these principles too far, and have too much prescription that isn’t fit for purpose, then you make life in the public capital markets more difficult, and people go private. And that has some negative flow-on effects.” He said the new principles would make it easier for companies to go to the public capital markets, but warned that excessive regulation was hindering that.
“If you have the objective of making the public capital markets more attractive, you would take a microscope to a lot of that regulation and law and try to wind it back,” he said.
“When you look around the world, directors of listed companies in Australia have more individual and policy responsibilities than in other countries. Over a number of years, we’ve overlaid more and more responsibilities onto the directors of listed public companies in Australia through law and through regulation.
“I think we’ve gone too far, and it would be useful to wind that back,” Dr Lowe added.
Mr Wylie, founder of the $3bn investment fund Tanarra, said simplifying corporate governance rules was a step in the right direction.
“We continue to believe that long-term Australian equity market performance would benefit from the ASX encouraging a greater ownership mentality in Australian boardrooms, and moving Australia into line with international best practice through annual full board elections,” Mr Wylie said.
ASX acting group executive for listings Gavin Skene said the principles would only work if they were not seen as a box-checking exercise. “Companies can apply the principles in a way that reflects their circumstances, while remaining accountable to investors when they don’t,” Mr Skene said.
“There are refinements throughout the principles, including simplifying the approach to director and executive remuneration, and in board composition, especially the recognition that a board with diversity of thought, experience and perspective can make better decisions.” Diversity reporting has also been de-emphasised in the simplified eight principles, with aspects moving from the first principle to the second.
The consultation paper also adds that major technological advancements, such as in artificial intelligence and the energy transition, would benefit more from diversity of thought than of gender.
“While the introduction of measurable objectives has delivered a material improvement in gender diversity on ASX 300 boards, a broad range of stakeholders increasingly recognise that effective board composition also benefits from diversity of skills, experience and background,” the paper reads.
“In this context, a broader mix of experience and cognitive perspectives can support more robust board deliberations and reduce the risk of groupthink.
“It may also strengthen board capability in areas such as technology, science and business transformation (in addition to more established disciplines such as accounting and law), which is relevant to emerging governance challenges including the energy transition and data and digital transformation.” The eight-member corporate governance advisory group was formed in November 2025, with former governor Dr Lowe its inaugural chair. Other members include former AusSuper investment boss Mark Delaney and Australian Retirement Trust chair Helen Rowell.
The ASX and the advisory group will soon go on a national roadshow for feedback, and is taking submissions for eight weeks until mid-September.
GOVERNANCE SOLVED 4th edition • 19-member Corporate Governance Council • 30 per cent female target for ASX boards • Extension of diversity characteristics to include race, sexual orientation, religious beliefs and socio-economic background 5th edition * 8-member corporate governance advisory group, led by Philip Lowe * 30 per cent female target for ASX boards retained * Additional targets for other diversity characteristics abandoned ASX principles simplified: 1. Lay solid foundations for management and oversight 2. Structure the board to be effective 3. Instil and reinforce a culture of acting lawfully, ethically and responsibly 4. Safeguard the integrity of corporate reports 5. Make timely, balanced and accurate disclosure 6. Support the rights of security holders 7. Understand and manage risk 8. Remunerate fairly and responsibly
